title: India Just Threatened to Roll Back Whisky Tariff Cuts. Britain's Steel Protectionism Is the Reason.
excerpt: The India-UK free trade deal, signed last year, is unravelling before it takes effect. New Delhi says if London does not lift its steel safeguards by July 1, the concessions on Scotch could disappear.
body:
The India-UK free trade deal is in trouble, and the dispute comes down to a simple question: can Britain protect its steel industry and still demand cheaper access for its whisky?

India has warned that it could reverse tariff concessions on Scotch whisky and other British goods if London fails to address New Delhi's concerns over new steel import restrictions, an Indian trade official said on Monday. The warning came hours before Britain's Trade Secretary Peter Kyle arrived in Delhi for talks with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal on Tuesday.

## The Steel Problem

The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, concluded in July 2025, was supposed to be the capstone of post-Brexit Britain's trade strategy in Asia. Under the deal, India agreed to cut tariffs on Scotch whisky from 150% to 75% initially and then to 40% over 10 years. In return, Britain would reduce barriers on Indian textiles, leather goods, and steel.

But Britain has since proposed new steel safeguard measures that will slash tariff-free import quotas from July 1, 2026, and nearly double duties on shipments exceeding those quotas to 50%. India exported roughly $900 million worth of iron and steel to the UK in the last financial year, much of which could be hit by the new restrictions.

"So now the ball is in their court," an Indian trade official told reporters. "If they do not leverage their free trade agreement, we can always reconsider the concessions we offered."

## Carbon Border Tax Adds Another Layer

India's grievances extend beyond steel quotas. The UK's planned Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism — which will impose levies on carbon-intensive imports including steel, aluminium and fertilisers — is another source of friction. While the carbon levies are still months away from implementation, Indian officials want them on the agenda now.

India, along with Brazil, Turkey, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Australia, has already raised concerns at the World Trade Organization over Britain's new steel import restrictions.

## The Kyle-Goyal Meeting

Following their meeting on Tuesday, Goyal posted on X that he and Kyle had "great conversations on charting the next phase of India-UK economic engagement, advancing shared business priorities, and further strengthening our robust and forward-looking partnership."

The British High Commission described Kyle's visit as signalling "the UK's determination to unlock the next phase of its modern economic partnership with India so it can deliver growth for people in both countries." It noted that bilateral trade is already worth £48 billion a year and that the FTA would liberalise 99% of UK tariffs and 90% of Indian tariffs.

Neither side announced a resolution on the steel dispute.

## Running Two Trade Fights Simultaneously

India is now bargaining hard on two trade fronts in the same week. While Kyle was in Delhi discussing steel and whisky, a US delegation led by chief negotiator Brendan Lynch was holding three-day talks in the same city to finalise an interim bilateral trade agreement. US Ambassador Sergio Gor said the deal is "99% complete."

The parallel negotiations highlight India's growing leverage — and its growing list of trade disputes. The world's fifth-largest economy is simultaneously extracting concessions from its former colonial ruler and its largest trading partner, while maintaining that both deals must serve Indian interests first.

For the India-UK deal, the July 1 deadline for the steel safeguards makes the next four weeks critical. The agreement was supposed to boost bilateral trade by an additional £25.5 billion ($34 billion) by 2040. Whether that number holds depends on what happens in the next 30 days.
nri_angle: The India-UK trade deal matters directly to the Indian diaspora in Britain — one of the largest and most economically active immigrant communities in the country. Cheaper whisky tariffs were expected to benefit the growing premium spirits market in India, while easier market access for Indian goods and services would create opportunities for diaspora-connected businesses. If the deal unravels, the effects will ripple through sectors from textiles and pharmaceuticals to IT services, where Indian companies have built substantial UK operations.
